html:
A handbook on running a country estate, written by Cato the Elder around 160 BCE. Its Latin title is De agri cultura, and it is the oldest work of Latin prose that survives whole.

Cato writes for a landowner with a middle-sized farm in Italy, growing mainly olives and vines for sale. The work is done by slaves under a slave overseer. His advice is blunt: keep the slaves busy, feed them by a fixed ration, and sell the old and the sick along with worn-out tools. The book shows the new kind of estate that spread in Italy as Rome's wars brought in cheap captives, the world that produced the First Servile War and the Gracchan land reform.

It is also a cookbook and prayer book. Cato gives recipes for bread, cheesecakes such as placenta and libum, and wine, and the words to say when offering to the gods before the harvest.

Later writers valued his plain, practical tone, and Pliny the Elder quotes him often in his Natural History.
sum: A handbook on running a country estate, written by Cato the Elder around 160 BCE. Its Latin title is De agri cultura, and it is the oldest work of Latin prose that survives whole.
